19. In Writ Petition No.5096 of 2019 it is contended that the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit on 30.07.2018 for importing 'Black Steel Seamless Pipe' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20; After arrival of the goods at ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-28719 dated 18.10.2018 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority raised dispute regarding the declared H.S. Code suggesting different H.S. Code and also suggested to examine the goods by the BUET for determining actual H.S Code; Though the provisional assessment was made on 21.10.2018 but the respondent no.1 sent a letter to the petitioner on 10.04.2019 asking to deposit required money for chemical examination beyond the period of limitation; Hence the petitioner constrained to file the writ petition. 

 24. In Writ Petition No.5097 of 2019 it is contended that the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit on 30.07.2018 for importing 'Black Steel Seamless Pipe' declaring H.S. Code No.7304.29.10 and 7304.29.20; After arrival of the goods at ICD Kamlapur, Dhaka, the petitioner through his C&F Agent submitted Bill of Entry No.C-28697 dated 17.10.2018 for releasing the goods as per declaration but the customs authority raised dispute regarding declared H.S. Code and suggested different H.S. Codes and also suggested that the sample of the goods is required to be examined by the BUET for determining actual H.S. Code; However, at the instance of the petitioner the goods were released on provisional assessment under section 81 of the Customs Act vide order dated 21.10.2018; After expiry of the statutory period of limitation the respondent no.1 sent a letter on 10.04.2019 asking the petitioner to deposit required money for chemical examination of the sample by BUET in order to determine the actual H.S Code; Hence the petitioner constrained to file the writ petition. 

 30. Mr. Morshed continues that from the pay order dated 08.06.2018 and test report of BUET annexed to the supplementary affidavit it is apparent that due to negligence of the petitioner in paying the cost for chemical examination and time consumed for chemical examination by the BUET the prescribed timeframe cannot be maintained. Furthermore, it is apparent from the test report by the BUET that the writ petitioner declared wrong H.S. Code for evading applicable duties and taxes as per actual H.S. Code of the imported goods but this aspect was not considered by the High Court Division in passing the impugned judgment and order as such impugned judgment and order is not tenable in the eye of law. He also submits that it appears from annexure-'H' appended to the Writ Petition No.4007 of 2019 (Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.279 of 2020) that provisional assessment was done on 06.09.2016 at the instance of the petitioner and accordingly sample of the goods sent to the BUET for determining actual H.S. Code wherein it is found that the declared H.S. Code by the petitioner was wrong and even the description of the goods was also wrong and the petitioner declared the wrong H.S. Code with wrong description of the goods for evading applicable duties and taxes on the actual H.S. Code. He next submits that due to negligence of the petitioner in depositing the cost for chemical examinations as well as time spend in chemical examination by BUET the period of limitation could not be maintained and this factual aspect was not considered by the High Court Division as such impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

 41. Similarly, section 81(2) stipulated the timeframe for making provisional assessment final with the word 'shall'. Section 81 provides that the National Board of Revenue may, under exceptional circumstances recorded in writing, extend the period of final assessment specified under this sub-sections. From Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos.278-280 of 2020 arising out of Writs Petition Nos.4006- 4008 of 2019, it is evident that though the provisional assessments were made at the instance of the petitioner's C&F Agent who applied in writing for releasing the goods on provisional assessment subject to ascertaining actual H.S. Code through chemical examination by the BUET/ BCSIR but from the annexures appended to the writ petitions it is apparent that the C&F agent of the petitioner did not deposit the expense of chemical examination in time. Moreover, chemical examination by the BUET/BCSIR consumed some time for which the timeframe cannot be maintained. Moreover, in the chemical examination it is proved that the petitioner imported the goods by declaring wrong H.S. Code in order to evade duties and taxes. Thereafter, the customs authority issued show cause notice upon the importer-petitioner referring chemical examination report by giving opportunity to reply and hearing but the petitioner without giving reply or appearing in hearing i.e. without exhausting the adjudication process invoked the writ jurisdiction. The High Court Division lost sight of this factual and legal aspect and thus came to erroneous decision in making the Rules absolute. Though there is statutory time limit under section 81(2) of the Customs Act to make provisional assessment final but from the chemical examination report it appears that the importer-petitioner intentionally tried to deceive the Government from realizing revenue by declaring wrong H.S. Code of the imported goods which tantamounts to practicing fraud. It is the settled principle of law that action against fraud has no limitation. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and orders passed in, Writ Petition Nos.4006- 4008 of 2019 passed by the High Court Division are hereby set aside.
